505.title: Mawlid: the Prophet's birth
505.hook: many Muslims celebrate the Prophet's birth with poems and gatherings in Rabi' al-Awwal, while others don't mark it
505.howItsDone: Many Muslims mark the Mawlid in Rabi' al-Awwal with gatherings, poetry such as the Burda, and charity, while others, following scholars who regard it as a later practice, do not celebrate it; nearly all send blessings on the Prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Husayn at Karbala, and your line was he stood for justice. Who did you hand a cup of water? Day five hundred five.

Someone once asked the Prophet ﷺ why he fasted on Mondays. His answer, recorded in Muslim's collection, was short: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation first came to me. It's the clearest word in the hadith on how he himself marked the day: he fasted. Centuries later, in the third month of the Islamic year, Rabi' al-Awwal, whole cities light up for it. And other Muslims, just as devoted to him, don't mark the day at all. Today, the Mawlid.

Mawlid means birth, or the time and place of a birth, from the root w-l-d, to give birth. Sunni communities often mark it on the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, and Shia communities often on the seventeenth. The sources don't settle the exact date. Public celebrations grew up over the centuries. Historians point to the Fatimid court in Cairo, and to Irbil in northern Iraq in the early 1200s, where a ruler named Muzaffar al-Din held huge gatherings with recitations and food for the poor. Today, in places from Morocco to Indonesia, people gather to recite poems in the Prophet's praise. Some sing the Burda, the Mantle, by the Egyptian poet al-Busiri. Others recite mawlid texts that tell his birth and life in verse. Mosques are decorated. Sweets are handed out. Other Muslims don't celebrate it. Some scholars, notably in the Salafi tradition, say that since the companions didn't hold such gatherings, the day shouldn't be made a festival, and they keep their love for the Prophet in following his example every day. Supporters answer that remembering him with joy and praise is good, even if the form is new. The disagreement is real, and serious people stand on both sides. What both sides share is the salawat. Surah Al-Ahzab says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." And a hadith in Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, God sends ten blessings on them. On the Mawlid or on any ordinary Monday, that blessing is one way Muslims keep him close.
screen: `MAWLID: BIRTH, FROM W-L-D.` · `POEMS, LIGHTS, FOOD FOR THE POOR.` · `OTHERS DON'T MARK IT.` · `THE SALAWAT, SHARED BY BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send salawat ten times. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you pray, say a blessing on the Prophet ten times, slowly. Many Muslims use the short form, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam, may God bless him and give him peace. If you don't pray, spend the time thinking of one thing about the Prophet's life you've learned on this path that stayed with you. The bell holds the time.
Mawlid. The Prophet's birth, celebrated by many Muslims with poems and gatherings in Rabi' al-Awwal, and left unmarked by others. Today's word.
Your line: peace on the one born. Today, whenever you hear or say his name, add the blessing, or simply notice the name. Day five hundred five.

506.title: Rajab: the night journey remembered
506.hook: many recall the night journey and the gift of the five prayers
506.howItsDone: Many Muslims commemorate the Isra and Mi'raj on the 27th of Rajab with talks, recitation and extra prayer, while others do not mark a specific night; the five daily prayers are understood to have been given during the Mi'raj.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mawlid, and your line was peace on the one born. How many times did you hear his name? Day five hundred six.

Before dawn, at midday, in the afternoon, at sunset, at night. Five times a day, in kitchens and offices and the back rooms of shops, Muslims who keep the prayer stop what they're doing, face Mecca, and pray. It can look, from outside, like a heavy schedule. A lot of obligations. But the story Muslims tell about where those five prayers came from frames them very differently. They weren't handed down as a burden. In that story, they were a gift, brought back from the ascent through the heavens. In the month of Rajab, many Muslims remember that journey.

Seven weeks ago you read the verse that opens Surah Al-Isra: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship". That's the Isra, the night journey, from Mecca to Jerusalem. The hadith collections tell the rest, the Mi'raj, the ascent through the heavens. Bukhari and Muslim describe the Prophet ﷺ meeting earlier prophets at each level, and then being given the prayer: fifty prayers a day. On his way down, he met Musa, who asked what he'd been given. Fifty, he said. Musa told him: your people won't manage that. I've tried with people before you. Go back and ask for less. So he went back, and it was reduced. And back again, and again, Musa sending him each time, until it was five. Musa said, go back once more. The Prophet said he was ashamed to ask again. And then, in the hadith, the word came: they are five, and they are fifty. Five in the doing, fifty in the reward. So Muslims who pray five times a day are, in the story's terms, carrying a gift that was made lighter for them, out of mercy, with Musa's help, and still counted at its full weight. When did it happen? The Qur'an doesn't give a date. Many Muslims commemorate it on the twenty-seventh of Rajab, and this is a widespread custom. But scholars differ on the date, and the early sources give several different months. Some communities hold gatherings that night; others don't mark it specially. What everyone shares is the prayers themselves.
screen: `THE ISRA: MECCA TO JERUSALEM.` · `THE MI'RAJ: FIFTY PRAYERS.` · `MUSA: GO BACK AND ASK FOR LESS.` · `FIVE IN THE DOING, FIFTY IN REWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray one prayer attentively. If you pray, choose the next of the five, and before you begin, remember where the story says it came from, the ascent, and the long back-and-forth to make it light enough. Then pray it as a gift. If you don't pray, take this sit as your own few minutes set apart, and spend them noticing what it feels like to stop. The bell holds the time.
Mi'raj. The ascent through the heavens, when the five daily prayers were given, after the night journey to Jerusalem. Today's word.
Your line: the prayers were a gift. Today, when one of the five prayer times passes, notice it, wherever you are, and take one slow breath. Day five hundred six.

507.title: Sha'ban: getting ready
507.hook: the Prophet ﷺ fasted much in Sha'ban (Bukhari), and some mark its middle night while others don't
507.tomorrow: Ramadan: the month of the Qur'an
507.howItsDone: Many Muslims increase voluntary fasting in Sha'ban to prepare for Ramadan; some communities spend the 15th night in prayer (Shab-e-Barat in South Asia, and for Twelver Shia also the Mahdi's birth), while others do not mark it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mi'raj, and your line was the prayers were a gift. Which prayer time did you notice, and where were you? Day five hundred seven.

Nobody runs a marathon without training. Nobody plants a garden in the same hour they decide to have one; first you clear the weeds, turn the soil, wait for the right week. Ramadan, a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, is a lot to step into cold. And the month right before it, Sha'ban, has a reputation among Muslims as the month of getting ready. 'A'isha, the Prophet's ﷺ wife, noticed something about what he did in it.

Bukhari records 'A'isha's words, roughly: I never saw the Messenger of God fast a whole month except Ramadan, and I never saw him fast more in any month than in Sha'ban. So it was his busiest month of voluntary fasting. Why? A hadith in an-Nasa'i gives his own answer, through Usama ibn Zayd. Sha'ban, he said, is a month people neglect, between Rajab and Ramadan, and it's a month when deeds are raised to God, and he loved for his deeds to be raised while he was fasting. Between a sacred month and the holy month, people relax. He did the opposite. And yet there's a careful limit. Another hadith in Bukhari says: don't fast a day or two right before Ramadan, unless it's a fast you already regularly keep. Getting ready doesn't mean rushing in early. It means training through the month, then letting Ramadan begin on its own day. Then there's the middle night, the fifteenth of Sha'ban. Some Muslims, especially in South Asia, where it's called Shab-e-Barat, spend it in prayer, visit graves, and ask forgiveness. For Twelver Shia Muslims, it is also the birth of the twelfth Imam, al-Mahdi. Other Muslims don't mark the night specially, because some hadith scholars have judged the reports about it weak, and say the Prophet's practice was the steady fasting of the whole month, not one special night. Both sides want the same thing: to arrive at Ramadan with the ground already turned.
screen: `HE FASTED MOST IN SHA'BAN.` · `A MONTH PEOPLE NEGLECT.` · `DON'T RUSH IN EARLY.` · `THE MIDDLE NIGHT, KEPT OR NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: train for something before it starts. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you fast, choose one day this coming week to fast as practice, and picture how the day will go: the early meal, the long afternoon, the evening. If you don't fast, rehearse one small piece of it instead: plan to wake fifteen minutes early one morning, the way someone fasting rises for the pre-dawn meal, and picture that. Notice what feels hard ahead of time. The bell holds the time.
Sha'ban. The month before Ramadan, when the Prophet fasted more than in any other month besides Ramadan: the month of getting ready. Today's word.
Your line: prepare the ground. Today, do one small thing now that will make something coming up easier: a list, a conversation, an early night. Day five hundred seven.

508.title: Ramadan: the month of the Qur'an
508.hook: Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with the Prophet ﷺ every Ramadan (Bukhari)
508.howItsDone: During Ramadan, many Muslims give extra time to the Qur'an, reading it alone or hearing it in the nightly tarawih prayers, where long portions are recited aloud; the month is also a time of increased charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sha'ban, the month of getting ready, and your line was prepare the ground. What did you do early to make something easier? Day five hundred eight.

Ask what Ramadan is, and the usual answer is: the month Muslims fast. No food or drink from dawn to sunset, for a whole month. That's true. But open the Qur'an to the verse that sets up the fast, and it introduces the month by something else first. Not hunger. Not the dates at sunset. A book. The fast is there, in the next breath. But the month's name tag, in the Qur'an's own words, is about reading.

Surah Al-Baqarah, verse one hundred eighty-five. Pickthall: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind". The verse goes on to say the Qur'an is clear proofs of guidance and the criterion, the furqan we met eleven days ago. Only then does it say: whoever of you is present in the month, let him fast it. So the fast follows the book. Muslims understand that the Qur'an's revelation began in Ramadan, on a night called Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, which we'll reach soon. And there's a scene in Bukhari that makes the month feel like a study partnership. Ibn 'Abbas says the Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people, and most generous of all in Ramadan, when Jibril met him every night of the month and went over the Qur'an with him. When Jibril met him, Ibn 'Abbas says, he was more generous with good than the wind sent forth. Another report says Jibril reviewed the whole Qur'an with him once each Ramadan, and twice in the last year of his life. So for many Muslims, Ramadan isn't only about what you don't eat. It's about what you take in. Mosques fill at night for the long tarawih prayers, where the Qur'an is recited in sections. Some who rarely open the book during the year try to read it all. Whatever else the month is, its first verse names it by a book.
screen: `THE MONTH IN WHICH THE QUR'AN CAME.` · `THE FAST FOLLOWS THE BOOK.` · `JIBRIL, EVERY NIGHT OF RAMADAN.` · `MORE GENEROUS THAN THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take in some of the book. Start small. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you have a Qur'an or an app nearby, read or listen to a few verses, slowly, in Arabic or in translation. If you don't, sit with the verse you just heard, the month in which the Qur'an came. Let it be enough for today. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The ninth month, the month of fasting, introduced in the Qur'an first as the month in which the Qur'an was revealed. Today's word.
Your line: the month of the book. Today, swap one scroll for a few lines of something worth reading. Day five hundred eight.

509.title: Ramadan: seclusion
509.hook: in the last ten nights many stay in the mosque in prayer
509.howItsDone: In the last ten days of Ramadan, some Muslims stay in the mosque in i'tikaf, leaving only for essential needs; others keep it for a day or a night, and practice for women varies between schools of law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramadan, and your line was the month of the book. What did you read instead of scrolling? Day five hundred nine.

Late at night in the last ten days of Ramadan, a corner of a large mosque can look like a campsite. Sleeping bags. A small curtain strung between pillars. A Qur'an, a water bottle, a phone switched off and tucked away. Someone has moved in. Not for a night, but for ten days, leaving only for what they truly must. They're not there because they have nowhere else to go. They have homes, jobs, families. They've stepped out of all of it, on purpose.

This is i'tikaf. The word means staying at something, keeping yourself to it. In i'tikaf, a person stays in the mosque with the intention of devoting themselves to God: prayer, Qur'an, remembrance, quiet. The Qur'an mentions it in Surah Al-Baqarah, in the verses about fasting, as people staying in the mosques. 'A'isha reports, in Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ used to spend the last ten days of every Ramadan in i'tikaf until he died, and that his wives kept the practice after him. Why the last ten? Because somewhere in them is Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. A hadith tells Muslims to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten. So i'tikaf is a way of being present for whichever night it turns out to be. Schools of law differ on details: how long it must last, and whether a woman may keep it in a prayer space at home, as the Hanafis allow, or in the mosque, as others teach. Some who can't take ten days keep a single day, or a night. And here's a human detail Bukhari keeps. While the Prophet was in i'tikaf, his wife Safiyya came to visit him one night. They talked, and when she rose to go home, he got up and walked her back. Withdrawal in this picture isn't coldness. It's closing the door on the noise, not on the people you love. Withdraw to draw near: the outer world gets smaller, so that something else can get larger.
screen: `I'TIKAF: TO STAY, TO KEEP TO IT.` · `THE LAST TEN DAYS, EVERY YEAR.` · `WAITING FOR THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `HE WALKED SAFIYYA BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small seclusion. Sit somewhere you can close a door, if you can. Put your phone in another room, or face down and silent. For this sit, the world is a little smaller on purpose. Let the breath settle. Then, if you're able, choose one evening this week to stay offline for a few hours. If you pray, give it to prayer and the Qur'an. If you don't, give it to quiet. The bell holds the time.
I'tikaf. Staying in the mosque in devotion, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan: withdrawing from the world to draw near. Today's word.
Your line: withdraw to draw near. Today, pick your offline evening and put it in your calendar, so it actually happens. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: Ramadan: the whole book
510.hook: finishing the Qur'an in the month, one juz' a night
510.howItsDone: Many mosques recite one juz' a night in the tarawih prayers to complete the Qur'an by the end of Ramadan, often closing with a khatm supplication, and many Muslims read a juz' a day at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, i'tikaf, and your line was withdraw to draw near. Is your offline evening in the calendar? Day five hundred ten.

On one of the last nights of Ramadan, in many mosques, something happens that the regulars have been waiting for all month. The imam reaches the final pages of the Qur'an. The short surahs at the end. Then the very last one, An-Nas. And then, in many places, a long supplication, the khatm, with people in tears, because they've just heard the whole book, start to finish, standing in rows night after night. It started on the month's first night, with one portion. Today, how a book gets finished.
screen: `THE LAST PAGES, ON A LATE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an is divided, for reading, into thirty parts of roughly equal length. Each one is a juz'. The divisions don't come from the revelation itself. They were added later as a reading aid, and they're marked in the margins of many printed copies. Thirty parts, one a day, make a month. Many copies also divide each juz' into two halves, each called a hizb. So when a mosque recites one juz' a night in the tarawih prayers, it finishes the whole book by the end of Ramadan. Some do the same alone, a juz' a day, in the morning before work or at night after the fast. How fast should anyone read? Bukhari records the young companion 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr wanting to recite the whole Qur'an far more often. The Prophet ﷺ told him: read it in a month. He said he could do more. In the end the Prophet said: then read it in seven, and no less. Another report says that one who reads it in less than three days hasn't understood it. And the Qur'an itself, in Surah Al-Muzzammil, tells the Prophet: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." Tartil, the word is: unhurried, each letter given its due. So the goal isn't speed. It's a steady pace that carries you to the end. One juz' a night. Thirty steps. Then, on a late night near the end, the last page turns.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS, EACH A JUZ'.` · `ADDED FOR READING, NOT REVEALED.` · `READ IT IN SEVEN, AND NO LESS.` · `TARTIL: IN MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark your progress. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of something long you've started: a book, a course, a habit, maybe this path. Picture where you began, and where you are now. Picture the end. If you read the Qur'an, mark the place you've reached with a ribbon or a note. If you don't, mark your place in whatever long thing you're doing. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan again: the month when many Muslims hear or read the whole Qur'an, one juz', one thirtieth, each night. Today's word.
Your line: one juz' a night. Today, take one steady step on your long thing, and stop there. Tomorrow, another. Day five hundred ten.

511.title: Eid al-Fitr: the takbir
511.hook: on the way to Eid prayer, Allah is greatest, sung aloud
511.howItsDone: On Eid al-Fitr, Muslims give zakat al-fitr before the prayer, often eat a few dates, and recite the takbir aloud on the way to the congregational Eid prayer, which includes extra takbirs; the wording and count vary by school.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole book, and your line was one juz' a night. What steady step did you take on your long thing? Day five hundred eleven, the end of the week.

The crescent moon has been sighted, or the announcement has come through. Ramadan is over. The next morning, early, families are up in their best clothes. Kids in new shoes. Someone is handing out dates at the door. And from the mosque, from the open field where the prayer will be held, from people walking down the street in twos and threes, comes one phrase, sung over and over, in a melody many Muslims learned as children: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Today, the sound of Eid morning.

The phrase is the takbir, from the root k-b-r, to be great. Allahu akbar: God is greater, God is greatest. Takbirat is the plural: the takbirs. On Eid al-Fitr, they fill the morning. Many scholars connect the practice with the end of the very verse we heard three days ago about Ramadan. It closes by saying God wants ease for you, and wants you to complete the count of days, and in Pickthall's words, "that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you". Magnify, there, is the same verb, tukabbiru: to say God is great. So the fast ends, the count is complete, and the first thing to do is the takbir. A common form goes: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahil hamd. God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God, God is greatest, God is greatest, and to God belongs all praise. The wording and the number of repetitions vary a little between schools and regions. Then come small things the hadith preserve. Bukhari reports that the Prophet ﷺ wouldn't go out on the morning of Eid al-Fitr until he'd eaten some dates, an odd number of them. He went to the prayer by one road and came back by another; scholars give several reasons, and a common one is that more people would see and greet him. The charity of the fast, zakat al-fitr, was to be given before the prayer, so the poor could celebrate too. And in the Eid prayer itself there are extra takbirs, in many schools with raised hands, their number differing between schools. A month of quiet effort ends out loud.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Eid takbir. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you pray, say the takbir quietly, in Arabic or English, a few times through, and let it get a little stronger each time. If you don't, just listen to the words in your head, or picture the street on Eid morning: the clothes, the dates, the voices, the crowd heading the same way. The bell holds the time.
Takbirat. The takbirs, Allahu akbar, God is greatest, sung aloud on the way to the Eid prayer and called out within it. Today's word.

Your line: allahu akbar on the way. This week went from the Mawlid and the night journey, through Sha'ban and Ramadan, to Eid. Today, take a different road home, and greet someone on it. Day five hundred eleven.
